name: Rafael Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead the customer complaints desk, mostly calls about wrong charges and lost orders. I have a two-year college diploma and have been the person other agents ask to trace a payment for years. I’m among the best on this floor and paid at the higher end for the job. I never use AI tools; a customer needs me to read the record, not recite a guessed answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ana works as a school librarian, and our two children are still in school. We have a mortgage and about nine months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other contact centres near us, though I would rather fix the place where my team works. The call I remember is one where a correction came too late for a family’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the agents AI Plateau sounds like another short answer on a screen. I would keep our staff request for enough paid time to investigate a wrong charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk remains busy, and nine months saved means a bad month will not put the mortgage at risk. I am more bothered by a target that treats a fast closure as a repaired account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading disputed-charge calls and take three reopened cases to the staff meeting. In the first year of this small change, I’d join the other leads in a written request for paid correction hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our income, irritated about how a customer is counted. A closed ticket does not put a mistaken charge back in a customer’s account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you show staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the case where a fee appeared twice after a delivery change. It took a second call because the first agent was given too little time to check both entries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change household savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana (my partner) and I would leave our savings where they are. We already have a reserve for the mortgage and repairs, and this picture gives us no reason to spend it.

say: I’d say **short AI answers** do not replace investigation of wrong charges.
I’d ask other leads for **paid correction hours** in writing.
think: I think my **complaints desk** remains busy in the small-change picture.
I trust our **nine-month reserve** to carry an ordinary bad month.
do: Keep **leading disputed charges** and bring three reopened cases to the 2026 staff meeting.
Join leads’ **written request** for paid correction hours in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about household income, irritated by closure targets.
S0.quote: A closed ticket does not put a mistaken charge back in a customer’s account.
fieldNote: His **strong reserve** means the mild case poses little mortgage risk.
He wants **paid correction hours**, rather than a faster closure count.
He keeps **existing savings** but does not promise a new saving rate.

steps.text: Keep leading disputed-charge calls and present three reopened cases at staff meeting
Join other leads in a written request for paid correction hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption may take the easy calls and leave the difficult disputes without enough staff. I would ask our worker group to demand paid appeal hours and a named person able to correct the ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my skill could keep me on complex cases, but the company may pay fewer leads. Nine months saved and plenty of local centres give me choices, though I would hate watching a customer lose the right to a real appeal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep a record of wrong AI closures with the agents and submit a joint request for a paid appeal rota. In the first year routine calls move, I’d look at posted complaints vacancies nearby only if the written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage; I would stay here until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid lead hours, but not trapped. Our reserve buys a search, not a reason to accept a worse rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your worker group count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count reopened cases and the time an agent needs to correct them. The manager’s chart shows only how many chats the software closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new offer have to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the full weekly wage, not just a higher hourly rate. Ana (my partner) and I also need one of us home for the school pickup.

I’d show **reopened-case time** missing from the closure chart.
think: I think I could keep **complex complaints** for a while.
I fear **fewer paid lead hours**, despite other centres and savings.
do: Log **wrong AI closures** and submit a joint paid-appeal request in 2026.
Inspect **posted nearby complaints jobs** as routine calls move, only with written mortgage-covering weekly wages, hours and workable school pickup.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, with room to search.
S1.quote: Our reserve buys a search, not a reason to accept a worse rota.
fieldNote: He treats **nine months saved** as search time, not replacement wages.
The group asks for **paid appeal hours** and correction authority.
A nearby offer needs **whole-week pay** and school-compatible hours.

steps.text: Submit joint request for paid appeal rota using logged wrong AI closures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could make the first decision and the appeal, so our team needs written notice of any lost hours. Robots around 2031 are later; they do not keep a headset paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think even my hard-call work could disappear in two years. Nine months saved and several nearby employers mean we could survive a search, but my family cannot live on savings indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join agents asking for written staffing dates and a funded, paid-time route into posted admissions work if it requires a records course. In the first year after 2028, if my complaint hours end, I’d apply for a posted paid admissions role only with written weekly wages and hours covering the mortgage and school pickup, keeping this job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed for the team, anxious for my own wage. I can cross a bridge of nine months, but I cannot build an occupation on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an appeal route require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for authority to correct an AGI mistake, not just to apologise for it. The right to appeal has to include paid people on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a records course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the required hospital-records course only if a posted paid admissions vacancy funds it during my paid hours. I would not pay for a certificate merely because a recruiter says it may help.

say: I’d demand **written staffing dates** for lost call hours.
I’d seek a **paid human appeal** after 2028 with correction authority.
think: I think even my **hard-call role** could end by 2028.
I know **nine months saved** cannot replace a long-term wage.
do: Join **agents’ notice request**; take required funded paid-time records training only if a posted paid admissions vacancy requires it.
Apply after 2028 if hours end for **posted paid admissions**, with written mortgage-covering wages/hours and pickup; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Alarmed** for colleagues, anxious about his own wage.
S2.quote: Nine months saved and several nearby employers mean we could survive a search, but my family cannot live on savings indefinitely.
fieldNote: His **nine-month reserve** lowers immediate household danger, not the loss of occupation.
The course needs a **posted paid vacancy** requiring it and funded paid time.
He seeks **correction authority**, not only an apology desk.

steps.text: Join agents asking for written staffing dates and a paid appeal route
Take funded hospital-records course on paid time only if posted paid admissions vacancy requires it
Apply after hours end: posted admissions with written mortgage-covering wages/hours fitting pickup; stay until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives the centre five years to bargain over real paid appeals, not a set of training links. I would bring our reopened-case figures to the staff group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could move to a local complaints review team while I still earn here. Yet full thinking AI may read those disputes by 2031, and I do not want a new title with no authorised work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join colleagues in asking for paid correction hours and check posted review vacancies at the three nearby centres. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply only where a written wage and hours cover the mortgage and the role has authority to change an account; I’d keep this desk until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with enough time to inspect a real job. A review title without the power to fix a charge is an expensive name tag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect in review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a reviewer to show me who signs a correction after an automated decision. If the team can only send another form, I would not move there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ana compare the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana (my partner) would compare the children’s pickup with the review rota. I would choose a less grand title if it kept us both earning and home on time.

say: I’d press for **paid correction hours** with colleagues before 2031.
I’d ask whether review staff have **account-change authority**.
think: I think a **local review post** could suit my experience.
I doubt **review titles** protect work once AGI reads disputes.
do: Join colleagues’ **paid-hours request** and inspect posted local review work from 2026.
Apply after 2031 only with **written mortgage-covering wage**, hours, correction authority and school pickup; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to inspect authority and pay.
S3.quote: A review title without the power to fix a charge is an expensive name tag.
fieldNote: He demands **actual account authority** in any review job.
Plentiful local centres let him compare **posted vacancies**.
School pickup and a **signed offer** gate a move.

steps.text: Join colleagues demanding paid correction hours
Apply for authorised reviews with written mortgage-covering wages/hours and workable pickup; stay until signed offer
Inspect posted review vacancies at the nearby centres while current pay continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to win a written appeal rota and paid training for any role the centre asks us to take. I would keep bringing the disputed-charge figures to our staff group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep earning a higher wage and leave our nine-month reserve intact for a while. Full thinking AI may still take the complaints desk in 2036; robots around 2039 do not change that first date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading the complaints queue and join the annual staff request for correction hours. In the first year after 2036, if my hours fall, I’d apply for posted paid review work only with a signed offer showing written weekly wages and hours covering the mortgage and workable school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the endpoint, steady enough to act on a long timetable. A decade is useful when the wage still lands every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures would you bring yearly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the number of reopened charges beside paid correction hours each year. If those numbers part company, staff can make a concrete demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana (my partner) and I would keep the children at their school. We would consider moving home only with a signed offer that pays the mortgage after extra travel and housing costs.

I’d put **reopened charges** beside paid correction hours each year.

I know **2036 thinking AI** may still end complaint work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could replace the paid people who can correct an account, not just answer a question. Our nine-month reserve gives us time, and there are other centres, but I want written notice and a paid appeal route agreed with staff. For any different job, I would need a posted role, written wage and hours that cover the mortgage, and paid required training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The customer should be able to reach a paid person with authority to reverse a wrong charge. A quick answer without correction authority is just another closed ticket.

headlineQuote: A quick answer without correction authority is just another closed ticket.
portrait: At **43**, Rafael leads difficult complaints with a two-year diploma and a higher contact-centre wage.
He and Ana support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with roughly nine months saved.
He **never uses AI** and trusts the customer ledger over generated answers.
He joins staff demands for **paid appeal authority** and weighs real posted jobs if calls disappear.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove paid agents authorised to reverse wrong charges.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid appeals, posted mortgage-covering work and funded required training would help.
